utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I hereby establish that the Chamber is complete again and was informed that both parties have a preliminary question to raise. Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good morning, Your Honours. We were warned by the Prosecution kindly this morning that we missed two deadlines in responding to Prosecutor's 92 bis motions number 14 and number 19. We checked, and number 19 is dealing only with one witness and we are not going to file the response to this 92 bis motion, but we are -- we were a bit uncertain about the deadline for the 14th 92 bis motion and we could kindly ask for an extension as of today for 21 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection to that. Can I inquire with respect to the 19th motion is it that the Defence has no objection or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we grant the 21 days, Chamber would like to first verify when the deadline expired before we give -- grant additional time, if you would do so, but we will decide this in -- very soon but also not until after we've heard the Prosecution's view on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has a standing position that the Chamber feels that in the interests of justice the Defence should have whatever additional time is necessary to file a response, the Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that's what you said already, I think, on page 1, line 21. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if my memory serves me correctly, the response was due on the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider the matter and we will let you know today, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the matter the Defence wanted to raise. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I wanted to alert you to what is going to be a unique filing today. It relates to two witnesses that -- could we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could the witness be escorted into the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, some 40 more minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Before we resume, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Groenewegen. I'd like to ask you something about the night between the 12th and 13th of July, 1995. Did you hear of any suicides in Potocari that night?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The next morning we heard about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about the number of persons who actually committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as numbers are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to move on to the 13th of July and I'm going to ask you the following: The men who had been separated were all put up in the same house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as we heard and saw, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did the house look like?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I remember, the house almost didn't have any walls on the bottom floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So could one see into the house through these walls that were actually not there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you testified in the Blagojevic case, is it correct that you were shown a video-clip and that you could not recognise that house?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could very well be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would kindly ask for the video that the Prosecution tendered yesterday, P1164, so I would kindly ask Ms. Stewart to play the video for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, could we pause now? Could we please restart with the audio because I heard that there is a sound track from the very beginning of the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can see yourself in this video-clip.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I must have been among them, but to this day I have not recognised myself among the peacekeepers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know what General Mladic said at that moment on camera and to the assembled civilians there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know, and through the translators there, did you find out that civilians were discussing among themselves whether they would leave or whether they would stay?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was incomprehensible for us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know which day this was?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, this was the 12th but it could just as easily have been the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you saw General Mladic on the 13th in Potocari. Can you tell us where you saw him in Potocari on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you just saw on the video, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was with you from amongst your colleagues? Who was in your immediate vicinity when you say that you saw General Mladic in Potocari on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the video, I actually recognise only two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did General Mladic stay there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Witness, you told us that you do not know what you saw, whether it was on the 12th or the 13th. Now, all the questions are about the 13th and you refer to those images telling us -- give -- answering the questions about the 13th. That confuses me a bit because is it now your recollection that this must have been the 13th or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As I just said, based on the video images, I couldn't say specifically whether that was the 12th or the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you therefore also cannot rely on these video images in answering questions about what happened on the 13th. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. I'm trying to answer the questions as best I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your view, on the 13th of July as well, were cameramen there and were they filming what was happening?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to move on to some more general questions about the period before the 11th of July, 1995. Is it correct that from your observation post, you could see Muslims leaving the enclave of Srebrenica, in order to smuggle food supplies and weapons? Also you could see them leaving the enclave and going into combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take it one by one. First whether they left, second for the one purpose, third for the other purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So did you see Muslims leaving the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never actually saw them leaving the enclave myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any reports to the effect that Muslims were leaving the enclave, first of all to smuggle food supplies, but weapons as well?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no official reports, but we were told that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that Muslims were leaving the enclave in order to launch offensive operations against the Serb forces and civilians?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, too, is through hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that at your observation post, you were often exposed to cross fire between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How close were the armed Muslims in the enclave to you? What is the point where they were at the shortest distance compared to your observation post?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking for myself personally, that was between 500 and 1.000 metres was the closest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You personally never disarmed anyone in the enclave of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, you never had an opportunity to see anyone else disarming anyone in the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I ask a bit of clarification. Witness, did you also see Serb forces near to your observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never until that time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you said you saw Muslim -- armed Muslims in the enclave at a distance shortest between 500 and 1.000 metres, could you describe in more detail what you exactly saw. Were they in groups, were they individuals, how could you see at that distance their arms, and what kind of arms were there? I take it one by one. Individual or groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What kind of arms did they carry or have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pistols and what to us from a distance -- what to us looked like long-distance firearms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "long-distance firearms"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything else than rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just follow up, please. Now, did you observe these people 500 to 1.000 metres from your observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was only during the patrols that we made of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand you. You said the shortest distance to you was 500 to 1.000 metres. Did you come any closer than that to them? Did you come and talk to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, absolutely. One of our assignments while on patrol was that if we encountered armed people, to pursue them and try to disarm them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in disarming them did you have any exchange of words with them to find out who they were and what nationality they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If during our patrols we could get near the people that we saw were armed, either at that point they no longer had their arms or we couldn't find them any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I must ask the question: How did you make a determination that they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To us, that was the way to determine that they were walking around inside the enclave and did not seem to be from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I'm confused, Witness. I have just asked you if you had any exchange of words with them to -- and find out their nationality. You said: No, during our patrols when you get near the people that you saw armed, either at that point they no longer had their arms or you couldn't find them anymore. If you can't find them, how do you make a determination what nationality they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you specifically mean the individuals or groups that we saw and had the opportunity to find and speak with them, it was by using the very little we knew of that language that we knew they were indeed the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I have one follow-up question: Do I understand your testimony well when I think that you're telling us that armed men walking around or moving around within the enclave, in your view, could not have been anything else than Muslims because Serb armed forces were at that point in time, that's before the 11th of July, were not moving around within the enclave? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us, or you testified about the theft of UN equipment and items that belonged to the Dutch Battalion, and you mentioned an incident where some petrol cans were stolen. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Someone broke into the warehouse where the petrol or the oil was and that was stolen; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, the oil was stolen by the Muslims. Is that something that was established?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To us, that was the most logical party that would have stolen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not have to submit any reports to your superiors about the deployments of the BH Army units in the territory which was under your control, which you observed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's extremely unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the case, then? Can you tell us, what is the truth? Did you submit reports?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not do so personally but all these unusual particularities would always need to be reported to higher ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it an unusual incident when you run into or find an armed group within the enclave? Was that reported?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was reported, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you report incidents of violations of cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did indeed always communicate special details about parties shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D909, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is your evidence on April 15th 2010 in the Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 21 in e-court, which should be 1186 of the transcript, page 1186. We need lines 5 through 9. [In English] And I will read in English: "Q. Well, let me clarify. Did you have to send the report on where units of the BH Army were deployed in the territory that you were keeping under control and whether they were complying with the agreement on the cease-fire? "A. In my personal experience, no."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you said in -- while testifying in the Tolimir case, was that correct, or is what you said today in this trial correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that I never had to make such reports. I think the response "no" refers to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present when such a report was submitted, either orally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So how do you know that they were actually submitted?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every so often we would receive a briefing about unusual incidents in the area, and what had been reported or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You, yourself, or your battalion never took any action in order to prevent offensive operations launched from within the enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak only on my own behalf on that, and that is indeed correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Such operations by the Muslim army from within the enclave, you never received any reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember anything about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All you heard was rumours that there were such operations carried out; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as concerns me personally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are all the questions I had for this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Hasan, any need for re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I suspect I will take until the break and maybe a little bit after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you will now be re-examined by Ms. Hasan. Ms. Hasan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Could we have P1160 displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday, and this is at transcript page 10513, you were asked in cross-examination about belongings that the refugees left behind and you confirmed that a few belongings were left behind in the compound. I'd like you to look at this aerial image and if we could just zoom in a little bit closer, if that's possible, and take a look down towards the bottom of the screen, just right in the centre, if you can see there is a house there. Do you see that there? At the very bottom at the centre of the screen. There is a line of buses and there appears to be one bus close to that house, and what looks like a tree. Can you see that in the image?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you're referring to the bus that is positioned perpendicular to the long line of buses toward -- in the direction of the house, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. That is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, this is, Your Honours, what we in this case refer to as the "white house."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, if you please put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm about to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, were you positioned at any time on the 12th and 13th of July in the vicinity of this house?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I walked past it several times along the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any -- do you have any recollection of what you saw?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All we saw was that men were being collected in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall when you saw that, whether it was the 12th or the 13th, or on both days?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was only on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Witness, now, is that what you refer to as the unfinished house or is the unfinished house a separate building?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that based on these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I can just direct your attention, the -- in the centre of this image you've circled a house and you referred to that house as being a house where men were taken to. Is that house what you refer to as the unfinished house or is this also a third house that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, that's the circle marked H. From what I remember, it's a spot where the white house should have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And just to confirm, as far as you can recall, you saw men being taken to the house that's circled and to the house that's at the bottom of the screen? Is that -- have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to avoid confusion, Mr. Lukic. Witness, when you told us about men taken to an unfinished house, was that the only house you remember men were taken, or were there more houses, in your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. From my perception, there was only one house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You described that house as an unfinished house. Is the unfinished house you described for us, is that the same house as you refer to a minute ago as the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that some confusion has indeed arisen as to what the actual house was based on an aerial. At the time I circled the house designated H was from my perception the unfinished house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when a while ago you referred to the white house in one of your answers -- let me just see, I'll read exactly to you what you have said. One second, please. You said in one of your answers: "As far as I know, that's the circle marked H. From what I remember, it's a spot where the white house should have been." Do we have to understand this, that when you're talking about the unfinished house and the white house, that you're referring to only one single house, irrespective of where it is at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I mean the same house there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, we can get rid of this exhibit from the screen, please. Witness, yesterday at transcript page 10504 in cross-examination, you were asked about the separation of men and specifically asked about the separation of men on the 12th of July, and in answer to counsel's question, you said -- you were asked whether it was correct that on the first day men and women were -- men were not separated from the women and children, and your answer was: "I stated that at the time. Now I don't remember it as well. But this must be correct." And counsel had referred you to a statement you gave on the 29th of September, 1995. During your Popovic testimony, you were asked the same question, and during that testimony - I'll just read out the excerpt - at page -- transcript page 2972 in cross-examination, you were asked: "Q. Can you explain the reason why you changed this statement of yours later saying that the separations took place that day as well, the separations of men? "A. At each statement, I tried to describe the situation as close as possible to the truth. If anything, I state -- if anything I stated is not entirely accurate, I would be happy to correct that. As far as not separating the men, I've revised that." And just a little bit further in the transcript, counsel asks you in cross-examination: "Q. Did you give a correct statement on the 29th of September, 1995, that the refugees on the first day of the evacuation were not separated? "A. That would not have been accurate." Do you remember exactly what you said when you were -- when you provided the Dutch debriefing statement? And that statement is dated the 5th of September, 1995, so before you gave the statement to the Dutch military police and the ICTY. Do you recall exactly what you said at that time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember exactly what I stated about that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read that to you. So on the 5th of September, 1995, you say, well, the statement provides: "He saw that Muslims" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you're reading from what exactly at this moment? Is it available to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's 65 ter 28862.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, we are usually not roaming around in 65 ter material but if we can have it on our screen, we can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: 65 ter 28862 at page 7 in English. Perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It can be put on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We have a hard copy in the Dutch version for the witness, if it may be handed to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Dutch version in e-court as well? Yes. Okay. Then I'll try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. I don't believe that's a correct page in the B/C/S. If we could go to page 8, please. I'm sorry, it's page 9 in the B/C/S and it's still page 7 in the English. utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, does that refresh your recollection, then, of what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were immediately present there. I never actually placed people on the bus, but I did help people right next to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And the tasks that you were engaged in on that day with respect to these evacuations, could you explain what those were?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember exactly in words anymore what the specific assignment was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. Mr. Lukic, have the questions in re-examination triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further. Then, Witness, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to this courtroom and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, questions put to you by the Bench and questions put to you by the parties, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was just a question you had yesterday about the initials of the witness on -- it was Exhibit P1159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can I address that now or after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, perhaps it's better to address it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, the exhibit itself was created during the Popovic case and at that time, the witness was asked first to mark the execution point. I have the transcript reference. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Explicit request by Judge Agius, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that raise any further questions? If not, it has been sufficiently explained where it comes from. I take it, Mr. Lukic, that we don't have to receive any evidence on the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think it's time for a break. We will take a break, and is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness after the break? And that witness will also testify in his own language, if I understand it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nicolai, I presume. Mr. Nicolai, before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you in English. If you prefer to make that solemn declaration in your own language, you are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can do it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Nicolai. Mr. Nicolai, you will first be examined by Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Vanderpuye is counsel for the Prosecution and you will find him to your right. You may proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I address you as Mr. Nicolai, Witness. This Chamber has the habit of not addressing people by rank or by title, and it's not in any way an expression of depreciation for ranks and titles but everyone appears before us as an individual person who gives testimony of the truth. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, General, if you could please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I'm Cornelis Hendrick Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And sir, just by way of background, can you confirm that you have given evidence before this Tribunal in the following cases: The case of Dragomir Milosevic back in January of 2007; the case of -- the Popovic case, rather, in November of 2007; and the Tolimir case in August of 2010?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for the purposes of these proceedings, can you confirm that you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor dated 18 November 1996?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 28850 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that's on the screen, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that the statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 18th of November, 1996?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just go to the last page, it should be page 16 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that your signature that appears underneath the witness acknowledgement?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, have you had a chance to review the statement prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I still had a copy in my files, and an additional copy was sent to me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the statement accurately reflects what you said at the time and was true to your knowledge when you made it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you to be asked the same questions related to the issues discussed in your statement, would you in substance give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I would certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move at this time to admit the General's statement 25 -- I'm sorry, I have the number. 28850, together with the associated exhibits that are listed in the exhibit sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, subject to the objections that were set forth in our responsive filing to the Rule 92 ter motion filed on 2 April 2013, I have no further objections and those objections set forth in that filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just check with you, Mr. Vanderpuye, the associated exhibits, they do not include the ones you would like to have added to your 65 ter list, or do they?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the list, they are included, Mr. President. They are 28851 through 28853.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And so I take it that before you want to tender it, you are first seeking leave to add them to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, that's part of our 92 ter application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, you objected to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, Your Honour, in our filing, the three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber grants leave to add the three documents to the 65 ter list and all the remainder will be MFI'd, the statement et cetera, and we will decide at the end of the testimony of this witness. And perhaps, Madam Registrar, if you would prepare already a list of numbers for the associated exhibits included the three new ones. If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: One correction for the transcript. Mr. Vanderpuye, at page 23, line 17, I think there is a mistake. You said, "They are 28851 through 28853." If that is correct then it should be corrected like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, otherwise we would have a different problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the numbers reserved for those documents are?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, first maybe number for the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, for the statement and then just a range of numbers for the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement, meaning document 65 ter 28850, receives number P1165, while the associated exhibits documents received numbers starting from P1166 up and including P1181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you prepare a chart with description and 65 ter numbers and provisionally assigned numbers. They are all MFI'd for the time being. Mr. Vanderpuye, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have a summary I'd like to read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The witness entered the Royal Netherlands Army in 1965. In February 1995, he arrived in Bosnia as brigadier-general serving as chief of staff of UNPROFOR's BH command under Lieutenant-General Rupert Smith, until September 1995. As Chief of Staff, General Nicolai was responsible for keeping the commander fully aware of current situations and dealt with day to day matters. He followed the daily situation, ensured that reports were timely completed and forwarded accordingly and made sure the command's functions were carried out. Throughout his tenure, General Nicolai had contact with BiH political and military leaders. He also dealt with military leaders from the Bosnian Serb side, including VRS Main Staff Generals Mladic, Milovanovic, Gvero and Tolimir. General Nicolai was directly involved in discussions concerning Sarajevo-related events, such as freedom of movement, humanitarian aid, the use of Sarajevo airport, and firing and shelling incidents. He recalled particularly a letter of protest that he wrote to General Mladic on or about 3 July concerning Bosnian Serb mortar fire into UN headquarters, for which General Mladic denied VRS responsibility. He also recounted a later request to General Mladic to investigate the 28 August 1995 shelling of the marketplace in Sarajevo which Mladic similarly denied. As concerns the Srebrenica enclave, the witness had regular contact with DutchBat commander Colonel Karremans and was well informed about the worsening humanitarian situation. Karremans informed General Nicolai about continuing problems faced by DutchBat because of convoy restrictions imposed by the VRS, these affected troop rotations and resupplies of equipment, parts, ammunition, food and especially fuel. In June, Karremans reported that these problems had become so severe that his unit could no longer effectively discharge its mandate. Convoy restrictions also severely affected humanitarian organisations. During the VRS attack on the enclave in July, General Nicolai spoke with, among others, VRS Main Staff Generals Tolimir and Gvero on several occasions between the 8th and 12th of July. He repeatedly insisted that the VRS desist and withdraw. However both Main Staff generals, Gvero and Tolimir, persistently and falsely denied the VRS offensive engagement. On 9 July, UNPROFOR headquarters issued a written warning to General Mladic in which General Nicolai took part. This was based on the VRS's firing into the safe area directly targeting UN facilities and causing civilian deaths during the ongoing offensive. Having reached within one kilometre south of the town UNPROFOR headquarters warned that the VRS should immediately withdraw at the risk of NATO close air support. When on 10 July VRS troops attacked UN blocking positions, close air support was requested but could not be delivered until the early afternoon of 11 July. General Nicolai spoke with General Gvero later that afternoon during which General Gvero falsely claimed that the VRS was neither attacking UNPROFOR nor the civilian population. Gvero further threatened that if the air attacks did not stop immediately the witness would be held responsible for all further developments and the destiny of the UNPROFOR soldiers and the civilian population in Srebrenica. Ultimately close air support was called off as the VRS had taken Srebrenica and because it threatened to shell the Potocari compound at enormous risk to the civilians gathered there. General Gobillard spoke with General Gvero that evening and Gvero said that once the civilians were on VRS territory, they would be totally safe and were welcome to leave the enclave. Mladic met with Colonel Karremans that night, General Nicolai noted that Karremans had been instructed to stay with the civilian population and to observe that international rules were followed during the course of an evacuation made likely because there was no food, there was not enough medical care or even protection from the weather for the people there. Following the removal of the Srebrenica population from Potocari on 12th -- on the 12th and 13th of July, General Nicolai remained engaged with the VRS Main Staff concerning the evacuation of the wounded, remaining in Potocari and Bratunac, and concerning the withdrawal of DutchBat from the enclave a few days later on 21 July. Mr. President, that concludes my summary. I have a number of questions for the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Vanderpuye. I usually do not comment on summaries but if you want to give the public a fair report about what is found in the evidence of the witness, I think that is a malcommunication between UNPROFOR headquarters and the local command in Srebrenica and was part of the statement as well. And also, you said if the air attacks did not stop, you had -- there was air support given. That is also missing in your summary. But for the public to know that that is part of the evidence as well. And that's the purpose of all of it, that the public gets a fair picture of what the evidence in the 92 ter statement is about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, as you know your statement is from 1996. So if you could just catch us up a little bit on what you've been up to. First, let me ask you, are you still a member of the Dutch military?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. I'm no longer in active service. In September 2004, I was dismissed due to my age. I was discharged due to my age. From 1995 until I left the service, I subsequently held three positions: First, I was commander of the operations staff, so operations staff officer within the army; next, I was commander of the 1st Division; and in conclusion, I was in commander of the training command of the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what rank did you leave with, did you retire with?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I was general-major then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could take you back a little while to Bosnia in 1995. While you were General Smith's Chief of Staff, in performing your functions, did you make use of a military assistant?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. As my personal assistant, I had a military assistant, Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your dealings with the VRS Main Staff and other officers, did you rely on the assistance of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, because I don't have any command of Yugoslavian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the interpreter which you relied on during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember her first name, Svetlana which was shortened to Lana.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about the humanitarian aid in the enclave of Srebrenica and of course the issues facing UNPROFOR, particularly resupply issues. In your statement at paragraph 39 you refer to resupply difficulties facing UNPROFOR. And you also talk about a particular convoy which left on the 28th of June and was headed to the enclaves but arrived essentially stripped of its material. Also you note in your statement that humanitarian organisations also experienced similar problems. So with respect to those humanitarian aid organisations, first, can you tell us what you mean by that? Because it's not indicated in your statement. What organisations?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In most cases, these were UNHCR convoys because we did not have much to do with convoys of civilian institutions, but we officially requested permission to displace UNHCR convoys across Serb territory. And to be complete, of course, also the UNPROFOR convoys, but those convoys were intended to supply the military. We had to request permission for those as well. Often such permission was denied and in many case, after permission had been granted, the convoy would either be blocked en route or only partially allowed to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to ask you if you can clarify something that's been interpreted into the record here. And I'm not sure that I understand you so perhaps you can help me. It says, page 29, looks like line 16 or 15, it says: "... we officially requested permission to displace UNHCR convoys across Serb territory." And I'm not entirely clear on what that means. Perhaps you can clarify that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: What it means is that we requested permission to move the convoys. The convoys needed permission to get to their destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps let me ask it this way: Did you ask permission to escort UNHCR or accompany UNHCR convoys of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. Generally, I don't remember securing the UNHCR convoys with UNPROFOR troops. They moved on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. But you were responsible for requesting permission for their movement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct. This happened for practical reasons because the UNPROFOR HQ was in contact with the VRS contacts in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the problems that were facing the humanitarian aid organisations that you alluded to in your statement, can you describe how severe, or maybe not severe, the problems were that they faced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, before we seek an answer to that question, could the witness first explain the plural humanitarian aid organisations, where until now I think we've heard about the UNHCR but not of any other humanitarian aid organisation. Were there other such organisations which were facing the same problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aside from the UNHCR, assistance was provided by what were known as NGOs which is short for non-governmental organisations and they also brought supplies to the occupied areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they face the same problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume they did but I can't state that exactly because they didn't process their requests for movement through our headquarters, so I didn't have a clear view of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, are you -- okay. Perhaps it would be helpful to put that up on the screen. It's 65 ter 28850. P1165, I'm reminded. And I think we will need to go to page 39 which should be -- I mean paragraph 39, page 9 in the English and 9 in the B/C/S. It will only take a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll just quickly refer you, if I could, to the second-to-last sentence of paragraph 39, which says: "At the same time, the humanitarian aid organisations were having the same problems getting essential supplies into the enclaves." Then you talk about fresh food. Supplies being sent to the enclaves were quite often ruined at the time that it reached its destination due to the same restrictive practices being placed on them by the VRS. So my question is with respect to this -- just this particular sentence, can you tell us what was the source of your information for that conclusion or that observation?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I had no view of what was happening with the convoys en route, at least the ones that were not part of UNHCR or UNPROFOR but what we did have an impression of was in what measure convoys succeeded in reaching the enclaves. That was subject to the observation of the present -- of the troops and UNMOs present so we could see what entered but I couldn't see what got stuck en route.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So with respect to this particular observation concerning humanitarian aid organisations, the information that you relied on came from where?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As far as convoys were concerned that did not move under UN supervision, the only information I had was from troops on the ground, so those were troops present in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how did you receive that information? Was it in writing, was it in -- by telephone? Was there a reporting structure in place for you to get that information? If you could tell us just a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. What was most important of all was daily reporting. That happens in every army. At the end of the day, a daily sit-rep is drafted listing the most important events of the past day, and usually concluding with an assessment of the near future, so the events expected in the near future. In those daily sit-reps, not only the daily fighting was stated but also the most important information about the supply situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me turn back to my question which was did you receive any information as to how severe, or perhaps not, the convoy situation was or the supply or humanitarian situation was in the enclave during the period of time that you were in Bosnia? And I mean the Srebrenica enclave, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. The supply situation was tracked very closely. And as a very clear example, in the very first week of my performance as Chief of Staff I was faced with the fact that DutchBat's food supplies in Srebrenica were nearly depleted. The situation that arose was such that even General Smith told the VRS commander that if no permission was granted to allow food convoys to pass, he would have supplies delivered via the air with all possible consequence that might ensue. Later, in my period, food convoys were generally allowed to pass with some regularity, so that while the food situation was desperate but not such that the troops were in danger of starvation. It was a different situation with munitions or fuel or spare parts. Those were subject to very rigid restrictions. With fuel , for example, the last fuel convoy that reached Srebrenica was in late February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, could I ask you to be very precise? You started your questions about convoys which the witness was able to tell us UNPROFOR and UNHCR. Then you moved to the other organisations, humanity organisations, where the witness told us that he couldn't say what happened on the way. Now, in your last question, you're asking about how severe the convoy situation was, the witness said he couldn't tell us anything that happened. The supply of humanity -- or humanity situation was in the enclave. And then the witness started telling us again about the first series, that is supplies for UNPROFOR and not humanity organisations. So I do not understand why you did not stop the witness there and say, My question was still focused on humanitarian organisations. Let's try to keep things clear what we are talking about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll come back to the fuel and UNPROFOR supply issues in a moment as I was about to say. But in respect of the humanitarian situation, that is the situation affecting the population of the enclaves distinguishing from UNPROFOR, did you receive information as to the impact of restrictions on humanitarian aid to the enclave with respect to them? That is with respect to the population, as opposed to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, it's implied more or less in your question that the UNHCR was not given because you're still talking about humanitarian organisations. We should be very clear on what was monitored by the witness and what he learned from the final result in the enclave. Are you including now in this last question UNHCR and the other humanitarian organisations or are you focusing on one of the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm focusing on the humanitarian situation as a whole within the enclave which may involve UNHCR or a number of other organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That should then be clear for the witness, the humanitarian situation as a result of problems with convoys, either UNHCR or other humanitarian organisations. That is what you're asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The local population in Srebrenica depended on aid from outside for its survival. The enclave contained far more than the original population. There was an estimated number of about 30.000 people in the enclave, and insufficient food was available in the enclave for them. So they depended on aid from outside for food, and most of that was brought in by UNHCR convoys and I assume incidentally also by convoys pertaining to NGOs. As for fuel and medical supplies, they depended on outside aid as well. Within the enclave, on the DutchBat compound, a supply of fuel was available intended for the local population. That was actually part of the UNHCR supplies, and even if no more convoys arrived, fuel was distributed from that supply to the local population, medical supplies was a painful situation. Wherever possible DutchBat did its best it could to issue medical supplies to the medical institutions present in the enclave from its own supplies, but generally the shortage of food was a serious problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Between the time that you arrived in February of 1995 and July of 1995, when the enclave ultimately fell, did the humanitarian situation improve in any way?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. The contrary is true, because of the many restrictions on moving convoys, the supply situation only deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention, if I could, to some of the issues more directly affecting UNPROFOR, and at paragraph 40 of your statement, you discuss the problems facing or concerning, rather, troop rotations into the enclave from May onward. And let me ask the same question: Between that period of time, May and July when the enclave fell, did the problem concerning troop rotations abate in any way?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. The contrary is the case. Until May, there were not really any problems with relieving troops, I mean troops that had been to the Netherlands for a brief period of leave. From May, problems did arise there, and that's how it happened that a large number, I believe nearly 200 military troops, were not given permission to return to the enclave after their leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was there any action that was taken by UNPROFOR in order to either stem or diminish the amount of troops that were not being allowed to return; in other words, in order to prevent troops from leaving the enclave and then not being able to return?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the very first thing that happened, and I think that is fairly logical, is that when it turned out that our troops were not receiving permission to return, we suspended the leaves of the troops still present in the enclave. So we did not issue any more leaves until the other troops received permission to enter the enclave, and that permission wasn't granted. The second thing we did, of course at all levels, was that we addressed requests to the HQ of the VRS to get those troops back in after all. But that did not receive a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Militarily what was the effect of not granting leave to the troops that were in the enclave? What was the effect on morale or the effectiveness of the troops?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As for the impact on the morale of the troops I can't assess that very specifically. Of course, it's unpleasant if you don't receive your leave, not only for the troops but also for those at home, but what's worse is that one-third of the manning strength of the troops was not able to return to the enclave, and if you have to perform tasks with one-third fewer troops, and originally there were about 650 troops in the enclave ultimately, only 400 were left, then you understand that to -- to keep an enclave of that size under control in a very hilly terrain that's difficult to see properly, you understand that that mission then becomes almost impossible to carry out. And we had great difficulty manning the observation posts that were still present but you must understand that there were 13 observation posts along the entire perimeter of the enclave, and that means that you have only very limited control of what is happening along those boundaries so you can't properly control who enters or leaves the enclave. And let me add something to that. At the start of my period as Chief of Staff, mobile patrols were carried out with APCs - those are armoured personnel carriers - but due to the scarce fuel, these had to be discontinued fairly quickly, and only patrols on foot were performed. Clearly, of course, when the number of troops diminished so much, carrying out foot patrols in addition to manning the observation posts was reduced to virtually nil.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you bring that or those concerns to the attention of the VRS Main Staff, and particularly to General Mladic? And when I say "you," I mean either you or your command.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. This was raised at various moments. There were moments when complaints arrived from the VRS headquarters accusing UNPROFOR of not doing enough first to demilitarise, and to disarm the Muslim troops within the enclave, and in addition that we were not properly supervising the fact that the Muslim troops were expected to remain within the enclave. They complained about exfiltrations from the enclave and being attacked in Serb villages on Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you, if I could, 65 ter 19 -- 19282, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We will need to go to page 4 in the English and it should be the same in the B/C/S if we've got all the pages uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to look at this letter a little bit, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and I recognise the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does it relate to what we've just been discussing concerning the troop rotations affecting, or the limitations, rather, on troop rotations affecting the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. This is not about the very last part of my previous statement but what I stated before that, when I stated that we tried to get permission at all levels of the VRS HQ to get these soldiers into the enclave. After all, this is one example of that. It's a letter to General Janvier, the commander of UNPF, so the highest of the commanders in former Yugoslavia -- excuse me, a letter from General Janvier. He's referring to the consequences of the reduced manning strength and urgently appeals to the VRS HQ for permission to admit those 170 troops to the enclave after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President I move to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just make one correction considering that I reserved numbers up to P1181, well, one of the documents that numbers were reserved for was already admitted in evidence. Therefore, reserve numbers are up and including P1180. So consequently, the document 19282 will receive number P1181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this letter, for lack of a better term, typical of the type of letters that would be sent to the Main Staff or to General Mladic personally regarding issues affecting the Dutch Battalion or UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That was done with some regularity. Of course, the subjects varied. This concerned the rotation of troops who had been on leave but the same held true for the supply situation, blocking convoys, sometimes it was about fighting incidents. If at a certain point serious problems arose, this was handled not only orally over the phone but also through letters or submission of protests or complaints that were conveyed to the headquarters of the parties concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see in this document that General Janvier says that almost daily since 27 April there had been refusals to allow clearances for the rotations of UN personnel. Does that comport with your recollection of the circumstances at the time this letter was issued?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That corresponds with my recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just go to the area of resupply that you spoke about a little bit earlier, and that was -- concerns statement paragraph 39. You mentioned just now and also in your statement that the resupplies were affected by convoy restrictions including food, ammunition, equipment and things like that. Can you tell us in terms of the degree of the restrictions, for example, what percentage would you say or could you say of what was needed was actually getting through for the troops to be able to carry out their duties effectively pursuant to their mandate?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact answer but from what I remember, somewhat less than half of what was really needed entered the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you, in terms of fuel restrictions particularly, in your statement at paragraph 38, you refer -- well you say, rather, that you were in contact with Colonel Karremans and that fuel shortages were in a desperate situation and denied right up until July. And at a certain point Colonel Karremans provided a report saying that his unit had not become fully operational or, rather, could not become fully operational because of them. My question is: Did you raise this specific issue of fuel restrictions with General Mladic or the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. As I've stated previously, that was raised on various occasions. One excellent opportunity to do this was when the VRS HQ complained about UNPROFOR's poor performance of duties. If they complained about attacks by Muslims on Serb territory, then of course we were able to reply that we had little view of that one because we didn't have freedom of movement, but especially because due to fuel shortages we were unable to patrol adequately and keep a clear view of movements within the enclave, so it was very difficult for us to check whether any Muslim troops left the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you, if I could, 65 ter 17891. And then I've got just a couple of questions for you about this one. First, do you recognise your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we can see here that the addressee is General Ratko Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this letter is dated 26 June 1995. I have just a couple of questions regarding it. The first relates to the very last sentence of the first paragraph where you say: I warned you of such consequences several times before. And in particular, you're referring to the effect of fuel restrictions concerning the ability to effective patrolling -- the ability of DutchBat to effectively patrol the area. When you refer here in this letter to several times before, about how many times before had you made this case to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know that. I didn't keep an exact record, but if you figure that there was almost weekly contact with VRS generals, then this subject came up in several of those contacts, but I couldn't give you exact numbers as to how many times that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Fair enough. The second question that I have for you relates to the second paragraph, where you have asked for VRS troops to avoid or to cease basically targeting UNPROFOR OPs. Do you see that there in the second-to-last or rather third-to-last sentence? It starts with, "On the other hand ..."

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to your recollection, it appears in the letter that there was certain activity directed against UNPROFOR OPs by the VRS. Can you tell us what the result of your complaint, observation, was in this letter to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, as with most, or I could in fact say all complaints, the response from the VRS was denying that UNPROFOR troops, as well as the OPs, were attacked by VRS troops. Nonetheless, they suffered regular shellings, sometimes from grenades but also ground attacks, and until 11 June, this was denied very strongly by the contact persons concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move to admit this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17891 receives number P1182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Vanderpuye, I'm looking at the clock. We are close to the moment where we should take a break. Would that be --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It would be a great time. I'm about to go to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would first like to invite the witness to follow the usher and leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As the witness is being brought in, I've looked over the transcript and also looked at my outline and I wanted to let you know that I'm running a bit slower than I anticipated. I understand that I've used about an hour. I'll try to pick up the pace during this session, but with your permission I would like to be able to update you on what my situation is at the end of the session, so that I can give you at least a reasonable approximation, if I'll need additional time. But in any event, I will not need a substantial amount of time, like another hour or something, but I just want to let you know that ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're encouraged to see whether you can get back on track again so that your report at the end of this session is of comfort to the Chamber rather than to alarm the Chamber, Mr. Vanderpuye. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, General. At your statement, and this concerns the events the attack on the enclave which you indicated commenced on 6 July, at your statement in paragraph 43 you describe the surrounding attack, and you describe also the killing of a gunner, a Dutch gunner by the ABiH, when passing through ABiH Defence lines. First let me just ask you generally if you recall the event.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I still remember it like it happened yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the gunner, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That was Raviv van Rensen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You refer to a document which is a note of a conversation - if I could have 65 ter 5747 in e-court, please - it's a conversation, a note of that conversation, taken down by Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's P1170. It's MFI'd, okay. Thank you, Janet. All right. I think we have it in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to this document, we can see in the paragraph, unfortunately we don't have a better copy of this, but the paragraph just below the evidence registration number, towards the bottom of the screen, and it refers to the BiH, LO, is that liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Was interested in the exact locations of the OPs in subject. And it refers to OP Foxtrot, OP Uniform, and OP Sierra. With respect to the soldier, the gunner, that was killed, can you just tell us briefly what the relationship of that event was to these OPs as we see reflected in this third paragraph of this document?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. First I have to correct one thing, the time of the phone conversation indicated at the top is incorrect because the incident occurred in the course of Saturday afternoon so the conversation must have taken place after that time. So it would more likely be 1830 hours than 0830 hours. So -- but otherwise, the text is entirely accurate. The relationship between the various incidents is as follows: On Saturday afternoon OP Foxtrot was attacked, and was shot at with small calibre arms and by tanks, it was shelled by tanks, so the commander of the observation post for the safety of his soldiers, found it necessary to leave the OP, he had permission to do so, he then retreated with the crew on his vehicle and wanted to retreat to the compound in Potocari. The BiH troops did not like it that UNPROFOR was leaving the observation post and wanted to block the retreat of those soldiers, so they shot at the vehicle en route to Potocari, and I believe that they even threw a hand grenade at it, and as a consequence the gunner was hit and also died en route to the compound. Now, how this relates to the other OPs in the immediate surroundings of Foxtrot Uniform were involved, these were not fully equipped observation posts, as we had throughout the enclave up to that point. No, they were improvised positions nearby OP Foxtrot, positions taken to be able to continue the tasks of OP Foxtrot from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you bring to the attention of the VRS Main Staff the circumstances or rather, yes, the circumstances concerning the surrounding of the UN OPs and the death of the Dutch Battalion gunner, van Rensen?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we explained that it was out of extreme necessity that there was a withdrawal from that observation post and we urgently requested that should this happen again elsewhere, that there be no shooting at the retreating troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We note again -- I just want to note for the record that in the second paragraph of this document, it refers to 1515 hours attack essentially on DutchBat APC from BSA fire, and I'd like to show you an intercept dated 8 July 1995 and it's timed at 1530 hours. It's 65 ter 25115.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, this is listed as being under seal on my list that I was provided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For one reason or another, our computer screens stopped functioning immediately, perhaps due to this but we have no computer evidence on our screens. Could that be fixed? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Mr. Ivetic is right, it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. There we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, this is the intercept I was referring to, and as you can see, it's an intercept dated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we deal with this, could I ask one additional question? Witness, you were asked whether you brought to the attention of the VRS Main Staff the circumstances concerning the surrounding of the operation -- of the observation posts and the death, and then you said of course we explained that it was -- you talked about necessity and that if it would happen again, that there be no shooting at the retreating troops. But it was not the VRS that had shot at the retreating troops, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was the ABiH, the Muslim troops, shot that gunner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you bring it to their attention as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, the phone conversation or the previous message displayed on the screen concerned conversation with the BiH liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My attention is drawn to the fact that since I'm listening to the Dutch channel, that sometimes I'm too quick in answering. Therefore, the transcript is not complete but I think nothing essential is missing at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
