utterances.text: General, first, do you recognise the conversation that is shown in this intercept? As you can see, it purports to be a recorded conversation between UN [Realtime transcript read in error "you and"] General Nicolai and one of General Mladic's deputies, 8 July, 1530 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you misspoke, Mr. Vanderpuye, "between you and General Nicolai," you are recorded as having said. Perhaps you should check that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just clarify that. This purports to be a conversation between UN General Nicolai and one of General Mladic's deputies, at 1530 hours, July 8. Does this conversation seem familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. And as far as I can tell from that brief excerpt, it corresponds with a conversation I had in the course of that afternoon with, I believe, General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to show you is page 2 of this document and it will be just about six lines up from the bottom in the B/C/S, at the top of the paragraph -- at the top of, rather, page 2 in the English, X, who you believe is General Tolimir says: I'm going to check what this is about, I'm not informed about the problem the general was talking about, but in the course of the day Muslim forces carried out attacks in that part of the front towards us. Can you tell us a little bit about this? First, in the reference here where General Tolimir says, I'm not informed about the problem the general was talking about, who was he talking about?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he raised the fact that the BiH Muslim troops in the enclave were using six UNPROFOR armoured personnel carriers. Well, of course, that was entirely unknown to me because it was such an absurd accusation that I couldn't possibly attribute any credibility to it, but the accusation was made, and I believe I said that we would inquire and investigate how this misunderstanding could arise, but I can still assert that it's absurd to assume that the UN would lend military equipment to one of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During this conversation, if we go back to page 1 in the English, it refers right at the very first paragraph to Svetlana. It says: We could not hear General Nicolai and his interpreter Svetlana at all. Do you recall engaging in this conversation with General Tolimir through the use of the interpreter Svetlana that you referred to at the beginning of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. All my conversations with the warring parties were with the assistance of this interpreter. Otherwise I wouldn't be able to communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so where General Tolimir refers to "the general," "I want to say to the general," or "the problem the general is talking about," is he using that term because he's speaking to Svetlana and referring to you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President I'd like to tender this document, 65 ter 25115 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we maintain our objection to this document as we do to the whole series of these types of intercepts. There are many authenticity problems with the same that are evident from the document itself including the fact that if they couldn't hear the general and Svetlana, how do they know that it was the general and Svetlana on the other line when it's not mentioned in the document. Also the document purports to not be complete. There is no conversation recorded from the side of the UNPROFOR and the closing part to this document indicates that it is not complete and some other individual is bringing this document. So we stand by our objection as to these types of intercepts without having the individuals who actually recorded the intercepts to explain these anomalies. They are not reliable and do not meet the standards for admission under Rule 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One of the reasons why I had the General look at the document himself is because he's a participant in the conversation. There is probably no better form of authenticity than to have a participant in the conversation attest to the fact of the conversation and its circumstances. So I think it is admissible under Rule 89(C) whether it's complete or not, and certainly that's a matter that Mr. Ivetic can address on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't fix the incompleteness, does it, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think the witness said - I'll have to find it in the transcript - but I think he said that it was accurate to his recollection. If you give me just a moment I'll look that up and see if I can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has decided it will MFI the document. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25115 receives number P1183 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it has the status of marked for identification and keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. Just for the record, we have managed to locate something at least relevant to this issue and that is at page 47, lines 18 through 20. The witness said: "As far as I can tell from the brief excerpt, it corresponds with a conversation I had in the course of that afternoon with, I believe, General Tolimir." I'll move on to the next document. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 44, General, you indicate that General Tolimir was the only officer available on 8 July. So first, I would like to know when you made the call at 1530 on 8 July, was it General Tolimir that you were looking to speak to or someone else?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, ordinarily, and this is how it happened, in 90 per cent of the cases the conversation was from one Chief of Staff to the other Chief of Staff, so ordinarily my regular counterpart at the VRS headquarters was General Milovanovic, but he can't be present 24/7 so now and then he was replaced by others. I believe, from early July, I did not reach General Milovanovic on the phone anymore and he was consistently replaced by somebody else. In this case, it was General Tolimir but that mattered little to me. What mattered was that I had a counterpart at sufficient level so that at the other end I would be given direct answers and decisions could be taken, and General Tolimir's rank was definitely sufficient for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. The document that I just showed you, the intercept P1183, introduces the intercept saying that General Nicolai was looking for General Mladic and since he was not there a person X responded. Does that comport with your recollection with respect to this specific intercept, that is the one at 1530 hours on 8 July 1995 that I was just showing?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I believe that that Saturday, my only contact was with General Tolimir, and I don't remember -- which I do remember about 10 June when in the evening at a certain point I spoke over the phone with somebody who was not a general. But I think that on the 8th and the 9th, I was consistently in contact first with General Tolimir and later on, on the 11th, with General Gvero. But that's easiest to check based on the reports of the phone calls I had with those concerned because they list exactly whom I spoke with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And those are the notes that Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter took that are referred to in your statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In this period, when the situation became so urgent, reports were drafted of all those phone conversations by my personal staff officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could just quickly show you another intercept, it is 65 ter 25116, it's dated 8 July also, and the time of this one is 1725 hours. This should probably be under seal as well. It should be. This intercept is number 513 which by the way is the next in sequence from the one I just showed you by the CSB, SDB Tuzla. And it indicates here a time of 1725 hours and starts with someone from the UN was looking for Mladic and since he wasn't there another officer, X, from the aggressor army, responded. About halfway down the page, we can see here a reference to van Rensen and it's written down with two Ss. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall first whether or not you were a participant in this conversation at the time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That afternoon, I conducted various phone conversations, not only with LSO of the BiH but also with the VRS, that was General Tolimir, of course about the events, the attack on the OP, but also about its consequences, because after Private van Rensen had been shot to death the problem arose as to how to evacuate his remains, and we wanted to transport those remains back to the Netherlands as quickly as possible but we wanted to evacuate them by helicopter to get them out of the enclave, and of course I needed permission from the VRS HQ. And I think that that's what this phone call was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would similarly tender this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would also object to this one on the same grounds. Again, it is only half of a conversation. We don't know how the entity involved recorded this information. And there is also on the second page in the English again a discussion that the -- someone from the UN who was completely inaudible, so we could state that the reliability and probative value of this document is put in question by these anomalies unless the persons who took these intercepts testify and explain the same to the satisfaction of the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do have also to tender with this document the audio, while there is an audio version of it. It's the same intercept except it's the actual tape recording. It's 25116A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, talking about these intercepts, is my recollection well that they are part of a written motion for admission from the bar table? And if I am not mistaken, I signed a decision on that motion this morning, and I see that 25115 and 25116 were part of that motion. Now I have to check whether we admitted them or not. Of course, the parties couldn't know, I take it that it is filed, but therefore, that's perhaps not a reason not to decide on the matter at this very moment and even for this one, not to assign a number depending on whether that decision is filed or is not filed. So therefore I'm a bit hesitant, both for 25115 and 25116, to say anything further at this moment until we have checked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just wondering whether or not if it's marked for identification -- you're right it would have to be assigned a number in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we would have to change the decision later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's clear for the record with the 65 ter number anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be a need to vacate that number at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, please proceed. Meanwhile we will later verify whether P1183 should be vacated or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 44, you describe a telephone conversation with the VRS headquarters of 1945 hours, also on 8 July 1995. As you indicated previously, this is indicated in a note of Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter which has a 65 ter number of 5591. What I'd like to do is to just put that into e-court just for a moment. It's P1167 MFI'd. And once we've looked at that I'd like to show you another intercept very quickly. This is the note that you've indicated in your statement. And we can see here that this is an information that was passed to the BSA or VRS headquarters by you at the time indicated 1945 hours on 8 July. In it, there is a quote written down by Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter that: I talked to General Tolimir this afternoon about the BSA attack on OP Foxtrot. Do you recall this particular note and conversation?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just for the Chamber's benefit, I would just like to refer to a couple of items that I'd like us to keep in mind, and one is the reference to the OP Foxtrot, the other to UNPROFOR positions, about 500 metres west of OP Foxtrot, because I'd like to show this intercept now which is 65 ter 25051. This is an intercept that was provided by Croatian authorities or from Croatian authorities, the military. And in this particular intercept we can see that it refers to "General Micolai" - do you see that at the top? - and also to interpreter Svetlana. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it says, S, meaning Svetlana, and it writes -- it says: I spoke to General Tolimir this afternoon regarding an attack you carried out at the observation post located at the south of the Srebrenica enclave close to Zeleni Jadar. Do you recall -- do you recall this, one; and, two, is the OP post located at the south of the Srebrenica enclave OP Foxtrot?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to answer all of that so specifically. If I look at the text, it corresponds almost exactly with the notes that Colonel de Ruiter made of my conversation, so I think it's the same message; that's my complaint that after OP Foxtrot was attacked subsequently, the positions 500 metres to the west of that observation post were also attacked because I was objecting strenuously to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd just like to focus you on -- looks like it's about 10 or 15 lines right about the middle of the page where it says "so, your forces circled two UNPROFOR positions." Do you see that? You'll have to answer yes for the record.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as I read now from 65 ter 5591 I'd like you to take a look at the intercept and it says: "Although General Tolimir promised that UNPROFOR and UN positions would not be attacked, now two UNPROFOR positions about 500 metres west of OP Foxtrot have been surrounded by your troops."

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The next thing Svetlana says in this intercept is -- in the intercept is, "It's happening again. I strongly protest and ask you to withdraw your forces immediately." In this reference to "it's happening again," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, in the afternoon, we protested about the attack of OP Foxtrot and now UN positions are being attacked again. That's the impression conveyed by it's happening again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the record, Svetlana says, "I protest most strongly and request that the troops withdraw from there immediately," which you can see in this intercept just at the line we have just been reading where it says, "I strongly protest and ask you to withdraw your forces from there immediately."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure how to deal with this. I have the same application, but to the extent that the motion is being decided I think I'll leave it at that and move on to my next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it part of that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can't tell you off the top of my head, Mr. President. I apologise for that. I can check it though at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number was, the 65 ter number was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll let you know in a second. Please proceed meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record also, this intercept is timed at 1941 hours, 8 July; whereas 65 ter 5591, Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter's note, is timed four minutes later, 1945 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, I'd like to take you to 9 July and very quickly at paragraph 46 of your statement, you refer to a report that Colonel Karremans sent to your command on or about 9 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record that's 65 ter 5750. If we could have that in e-court very briefly. I'm sorry, it was MFI'd as P1152.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this the report that was sent to your command by Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 2 in the English and the B/C/S, please. In this document, you can see that Colonel Karremans provides background information concerning the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, in order to avoid any misunderstandings, 65 ter 05750 was marked for identification as P1173, not P1152.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, in this document, you can see that Colonel Karremans provides background of the situation, describes the attack at page 1, and then he talks about the situation on page 2 concerning the OP crews, the APCs that you refer to, and the situation around the enclave and describes the shelling of the Swedish shelter project in the south. Does that all comport with your recollection of this -- of the events?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At paragraph 9, which is what I'd like to refer you to specifically, Colonel Karremans writes of the BSA, or VRS, that if they manage to reach their objective, which in my opinion they can in due time, then two possible goals are left, firstly the conquest of the entire enclave, and secondly the enhancement of the occupation of the southern part. So my questions are these: One, did your command share Colonel Karremans' assessment in this respect?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That's basically correct, but we spent some days guessing at what the ultimate objective was of the attack by the VRS, and there were two options: One, the VRS would settle for merely occupying the southern section of the enclave, which was crossed by an important supply route; or they wanted to take the entire enclave, and that would yield the benefit that they would no longer need any troops controlling the surroundings of the enclave. It's always very difficult to ascertain what the actual objective is. For a very long time we thought that the VRS would settle for just the southern section of the enclave, but in retrospect, we were mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you with respect to paragraph 10 concerning Colonel Karremans' assessment of the use of close air support which you can see he's indicated there that it was not feasible yet. And he lays out a couple of reasons for that. Did your command share his assessment with respect to the use of close air support at this particular time, and this is on 9 July?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to remind you what Colonel Karremans based this assessment on. When air force had been used previously by the UN - I'm referring to the incidents on 25 and 26 May - the VRS responded very violently to the air strikes, and all enclaves were heavily shelled and shot at by the VRS, specifically there was a blood bath in the city of Tuzla in which over 80 civilians were killed and a few hundred injured. Colonel Karremans was worried that if the UN were to use air power in Srebrenica, similar response would follow and all the means available to the VRS surrounding the enclave would be used to shoot at the enclave with disastrous consequences for both the civilian population and possibly the military troops within the enclave as well. That's why he said if we were to consider using air power, then we would need to attack all -- attack and neutralise all positions surrounding the enclave immediately to prevent such a response from being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so was Lieutenant Karremans' assessment informed by the policy undertaken by the UNPROFOR command concerning guidance following these air strikes, that you refer to in paragraph 35 of your statement? If you need to, I can put that up on the screen to help you remember, or if you can remember, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I don't fully understand your question. What I can say about this is that as UNPROFOR staff, we understood this assessment by Karremans, but I might add immediately that close air support would exclude this opportunity to shoot all surrounding positions at the same time. You can use close air support only against weapons being deployed at that time. So you can use it retroactively but not preventively. And then because otherwise you're not referring to close air support but air strikes, and that was not within the competence of UNPROFOR or UNPF to carry that out. General Janvier could sanction close air support but only the UN HQ in New York could approve air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. At your statement, at paragraph 47, you note a series of phone calls again with General Tolimir, the first of which occurs at 1230, I believe, 9 July. And in particular you refer to the note taken by Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter - which for the benefit of the Chamber is 65 ter 5748 - if we could have that up on the screen for just a moment. It is MFI'd as P1171. Okay. First do you recognise this document? It's dated 9 July, timed at 1230 hours and signed by Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise the document, and I recognise the signature of my military assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in this document, we can see that it refers to a telephone conversation between you and General Tolimir and it refers to a number of items that I'll quickly point out, one is General Tolimir expressing his condolences for the death of the soldier in Srebrenica. Is that Mr. van Rensen as you indicated previously?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The second is in the third paragraph: General Nicolai concluded that he expected his soldiers would be allowed to return to their base today. Do you recall what that concerned?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. There were soldiers that had manned observation posts that had been attacked by the VRS, earlier on that day, when they were shot at by the BiH, that's the Muslim soldiers, when they were retreating, the soldiers preferred to surrender to the VRS, so to the Serbs, that happened in several cases. Those soldiers were subsequently transported away, I believe, to Bratunac. My request refers to that. I ask General Tolimir whether he could enable these soldiers to return as quickly as possible to the compound in the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in the last paragraph we see two things I'd like to note. One is that General Tolimir responded that he was not aware of his subordinate commanders obstructing the case evac or casualty evacuation by road. Does that refer to Mr. van Rensen?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. An agreement had been reached about transporting the remains of Private Rensen. He would be brought to a spot where the helicopter would land and during the transport, along the road, the convoy was blocked and that's what this discussion with General Tolimir is about, and he says that he'll check into that and will order that the transport be continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you an intercept, 25 -- no, I'm sorry, let me give you the -- 25118. That's the 65 ter number. It's the same date, 9 July, timed at 1240 hours, ten minutes later than the time indicated on the note. And here we can see that this is a -- should be under seal as well. I'm sorry if I didn't mention that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, we are close to a break anyhow. I don't know how much time you need to start with this. Otherwise we will take the break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should take me two minutes, hopefully, to get through this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take those two minutes and take a break then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you can see, General, this is an intercept timed at 1240 as I indicated. It says, once again, General Nicolai was inaudible. If we go to page 2 in the English, yes, then we will see X speaking and saying: Good afternoon to you, greetings to you and General Nicolai too. And the next time you see your name in the transcript, about midway through, it reads, the general -- I'm sorry: Once more, regards to General Nicolai. Please accept my condolences for the death of the UN staff member in Srebrenica. The last paragraph of the last five lines or so of the page it says: I'm not informed that my commanders prevented the evacuation of the body by land and would ask general to send by land his team towards Bratunac and I would immediately order that they are accepted and escorted to Zvornik and says, as he does in the note, I'm going to issue necessary orders immediately so that the Muslims cannot listen to it and create obstacles. Does this comport with your recollection of the conversation that is in the note recorded by Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter, 1230, 9 July?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That text corresponds almost exactly. These transcriptions as are being projected now are likely to be the literal report, de Ruiter always drafted a summary of the contents of a conversation. And the time is roughly the time at which the conversation took place. If you wanted to be very precise, you would need to indicate the start and the end of the phone call, but for understandable reasons, that didn't happen. So this corresponds with the message shown previously with respect to the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, general.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President I indicated a little earlier that I would need a little bit more time and I think I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much more would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would say probably not more than a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic one of the concerns that the Chamber might have is whether we would be able to conclude the testimony of this witness tomorrow. If Mr. Vanderpuye would need another half an hour, that would take, then, almost the whole of today's session. Would you be able to cross-examine the witness in tomorrow's session or would that not be sufficient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have four hours of cross-examination. I believe that we do not have four hours tomorrow of court time. I think the math is just under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, the Chamber grants you ten, at a maximum 15 minutes after the break, so therefore reorganise your further examination. Witness, we take a break. Mr. Nicolai, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I put on the record that 65 ter 25115, 25116, 25118, and 25051, that's four documents, are all part of the decision which is meanwhile filed although not yet distributed, in which these documents are -- it is distributed now as well, I do understand. Therefore P1183 can be vacated. Mr. Vanderpuye, you also talked about an audio, 25116A. I do not know -- as a matter of fact, I can't see whether that's covered by the decision, most likely not. So we'll check that first and then the tendering of 25116A is pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate that. I just wanted to know if there is a way for me to know -- never mind, I'll sort it out. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take a break and resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Vanderpuye, I'll be rather strict. Everyone is aware that we lost an hour this week. Everyone is also aware that Dutch interpreters are there for two days so we should all make serious efforts to stay well within the time limits. Perhaps in this respect, Mr. Ivetic, also in relation to making use of our time, if a witness has not told us that he has received special training in VRS structures, et cetera, the Chamber will not assume that he will have, what has not been said by the witness, and it's a line of questioning which is repeatedly appearing. Therefore, if it has not been positively established, the Chamber will not assume anything in that respect. Mr. Vanderpuye, you have until 5 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, I'll skip up to 11 July. We left off at 9 July and your statement does mention a series of conversations that you had with the members of the Main Staff but particularly General Tolimir and General Gvero so let me move to the 11th of July very quickly. In your statement, at paragraph 35, you refer to a conversation that you had with General Gvero, 1615 hours on the 11th. In that paragraph of your statement you say that: "He threatened me by saying that I would be held responsible for all further developments, the destiny of my men and the civilian population in Srebrenica." And you refer specifically to Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter's note corresponding to that time. I'll show you 65 ter 20918, which again is an intercepted communication and should be under seal. This intercept is, as you can see dated 11 July 1995. The time indicated is 1610 hours, report number 534, and it begins with an introduction of a conversation between General Gvero and General Nicolai who we did not hear. And the conversation goes as follows: The first thing I'd like to draw your attention to is General Gvero's statement that it's not true that our forces, meaning VRS forces, attacked UN soldiers. Is that something that was consistent with your knowledge of events on the ground at the time that you had the conversation with General Gvero. First, if you can confirm that you had the conversation as indicated in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Excuse me, yes, I conducted that conversation with General Gvero and even now after 18 years I am still angry that there was a situation that the UN had been attacked by VRS troops for five consecutive days and still on the afternoon of the 11th, General Gvero firmly denied that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you go a little bit further down the page in this intercept, he says, that is General Gvero, it's not appropriate to look for excuses like this to attack our forces unprovoked. First, did the UN attack VRS forces and second, was -- if there was such an attack, was it unprovoked, according to your recollection of the events on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. General Gvero refers to the fact that General Rensen, excuse me, Private Rensen was killed by the Muslims and he also alleges that the soldiers that surrendered to the VRS, the soldiers that fled their observation posts, he says that they were well treated by the VRS and that's also true. But he firmly denies that they were attacking and shooting at observation posts for several days directly firing at them and with other arms. It's not for nothing that they left the observation posts. He is simply ignoring that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And lastly on this same page with respect to General Gvero's third point where he says in case General Nicolai doesn't order the bombing to stop and doesn't withdraw NATO air planes he will have personal responsibility for the further developments and the destiny of all people in the area. First, did you have the power to order that bombings stop?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. I could exert some influence, but please remember that I was the Chief of Staff, not the commanding officer. In the absence of General Smith, the highest-ranking general, and deputy commander at that time was General Gobillard, who of course was in the same building where I was present as well, so I could help with decision-make but I was not the person who had the ultimate authority to that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how did you understand General Gvero's threat as you described it in your statement at paragraph 55? How did you understand it that he said you would be personally responsible for further developments and the destiny of all people in the area? How did you understand that to be a threat, as you've characterised it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that I was being held personally responsible did not impress me at all, but we did experience a threat. I deliberately say we, both General Gobillard and I, took that threat very seriously. On the one hand, threats were expressed in the enclave that were more specific than those stated by General Gvero, but given the memory of the retaliation acts at the end of May, it seemed very likely that if we did not desist from the air strikes, the enclave would come under heavy firing with all kinds of consequences for the massive concentration of refugees in and around the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this particular intercept as I don't see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 2900, you're talking about 2918 is part of the decision and was admitted into evidence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have five minutes. That's good to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, with respect to your statement at paragraph 65, you indicated that in your discussions with General Mladic, related to the departure of Dutch Battalion on 21 July, that General Mladic agreed to allow you to inspect the areas of Srebrenica and Bratunac. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: You mean on the date that DutchBat was to leave the enclave, the 21st?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I could put your statement up if you'd like to see it. That might be more helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's P1165. We will have to go to page 15 in the English and it should be at the bottom of page 14 on to page 15 in B/C/S. Okay. If we go to the very top of the page, in the English, I think we will have to start at the bottom. Yes, that's it in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We will see on 21 July, Dutch soldiers were to be evacuated from Srebrenica and says that this was a result of an agreement reached with Mladic and senior officers from both parties were to be represented at the event. We can see that in the first couple of sentences in the paragraph. It says: On my way to Srebrenica I was stopped at a Serb check-point where Mladic was waiting for me. We arrived at Srebrenica together, then we went to Bratunac just outside the enclave where we had a meal and discussed the conditions of departure of DutchBat. And then it says: Mladic offered during our discussions to let me make a tour of Srebrenica and Bratunac so I can inspect the situation after DutchBat had left. That's what I'm referring to specifically. Does that help you recall the event?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that entirely, but the weekend prior to that, there was a conference in Zagreb attended by both General Smith and General Mladic where various agreements were reached including DutchBat's departure later on Wednesday, I believe, on the 18th. That was confirmed in a meeting between General Mladic and General Smith, and in that encounter, it was agreed specifically that the UN parties present at that departure would have the opportunity to look around Srebrenica and Bratunac and to inspect the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to inspect Srebrenica, Bratunac surroundings, as General Mladic had indicated that you would be allowed to do?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Only partially. After DutchBat's evacuation had taken place, General Mladic said that he was pressed for time and that he would only be able to show me Srebrenica and the immediate surroundings, but had no time to let me look around in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said I have one question, you're now putting the third question to the witness. I said you have five minutes. Five minutes are over. That's exactly what I was meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, it's just the witness raised one issue with respect to General Mladic's conduct which I thought would be of relevance to the Chamber, but I can leave that to Mr. Ivetic or to redirect examination if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Then, Witness, I have to be strict on time. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, General. I would like to move immediately to my questions for the sake of time. To begin with, in your Rule 92 ter statement, which is P1165 marked for identification, at paragraph 2, which is page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S, you describe that you underwent both a training course in the Netherlands Institute of International Relations on the background and history of the conflict as well as a military peacekeeping course. The question I have for you is if these courses were offered by the same entity or if the second one was taught by some other entity?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: There was also a course at the training centre for peace missions, and that also covered a bit about the history but the main training was at the Clingendael Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And as I understand it, you were not a part of the DutchBat battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as I understand it, the training courses for DutchBat were supposed to take one year of time before deployment whereas yours took just about one month. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. But I need to explain that. I was being prepared specifically to operate in a specific position, namely Chief of Staff, within UNPROFOR. I did not need training to be suitable for operating as a general. These DutchBat soldiers received comprehensive training, first military training to act as military troops, plus additional training to operate in specific peace missions, and that requires far more than brief follow-up training targeting a specific position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, once you became Chief of Staff of BH command in Sarajevo, did you have occasion to verify or oversee if in fact the DutchBat personnel in Srebrenica had all received the requisite one year prior training prior to their deployment?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. It wasn't necessary and that's not my responsibility. It's the responsibility of the Dutch commander to ensure that his troops had had received the required training prior to deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now ask you about the last line in this same paragraph, paragraph 2 of your Rule 92 ter statement, wherein you say: Before I left for Bosnia I received a lot of reading material, and then you identify certain things. I want to ask you from whom did you receive this material? Was it from an official source or from an unofficial source?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I received the overwhelming majority from an official source. These are documents that were made available to me on behalf of the commander of the ground forces, but I remember that in addition to that I read books and the books that I did not own I received from friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one clarification, sir. You say that you -- they were made available to you on behalf of the commander of the ground forces. Could you identify which commander of which ground forces?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: There was only one commander of the ground forces, and that was General Kuzi [phoen] at the time, but I admit that I did not speak personally with General Kuzi but I did speak with his deputy, General van Baal, and he ensured that on behalf of the operations staff -- these documents were issued by the operations staff under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could ask you, sir, during the course of your deployment to Sarajevo, did you or any of the other members of the UNPROFOR BH command receive situation reports from NATO in addition to the United Nations sit-reps?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: We did not receive sit-reps from NATO. The sit-reps we received were the sit-reps of sectors under UNPROFOR command, and we received copies of sit-reps drafted in Zagreb so the level above us so those were the documents we received officially but if I want to be truly complete, and this also concerns obtaining intelligence, there was some contact with NATO, especially G-2, that's the intelligent officer on the staff, who was in contact with the HQ in Naples as well as with the US fleet section in the Adriatic, and they received information about that. So that was intelligence from NATO sources gathered by NATO air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try to break this down one item by one item. First of all, you've identified a G-2 individual in the headquarters. Am I correct that we are talking about Lieutenant-Colonel Powers?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And from which country did this individual come from prior to serving as a member of the BH command of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: He came from the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that you identified him at the level of the HQ. Am I correct that in addition to the BH command, that every unit in UNPROFOR had an intelligence officer who maintained contact with, as you said, the NATO HQ in Naples and had access to NATO satellite and other reconnaissance just as the G-2 at the headquarters at the BH command?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, I'll try to answer it as follows, and if this isn't enough, please let me know. Each level or NATO unit had an intelligence officer, a staff officer responsible for gathering intelligence, and that is G-2, or at lower levels the S-2. To obtain intelligence we had few resources available and depended on others. At the level of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, we were authorised to contact HQ in Naples as well several US units that I just mentioned. This was not the case for the levels below UNPROFOR, so lower than UNPROFOR. My G-2 was authorised to do this and I assumed that the G-2 in Zagreb was also authorised to this effect but levels below that did not have those sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One point of clarification, sir. You started off your answer by saying each level or NATO unit had an intelligence officer. Did you in fact mean to say each level or UN unit had an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you remember, who would have been the intelligence officer or officers assigned and operating as part of the DutchBat in Srebrenica during the time period of your deployment?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I definitely don't remember a name of such a person and I was not in contact with them. It was two levels below UNPROFOR so it was already remarkable that I was in contact with the DutchBat commander, certainly not with his S-2. It was probably a captain from his staff but I definitely don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And earlier, you said that -- you referred to your G-2. Am I correct that the intelligence service within the UNPROFOR BH command designated as the G-2 branch came under your direct command as Chief of Staff of the BH command?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that within your position, you had occasion to deal with Generals Gobillard and Janvier, and that both of these generals relied heavily on the use of English translators?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. General Gobillard hardly knew any English and General Janvier was a bit more proficient but not sufficiently proficient to operate without an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And am I also correct that the translator that you identified in direct examination, the individual named Svetlana, that you used this translator always when dealing with Serbo-Croat speakers, that it was always the same translator that you used?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, always might be an exaggeration, but I did in 90 per cent of the cases. Very rarely if something happened at a time when Svetlana was not present we would sometimes need to use one of the military interpreters present at the HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And your military assistant, Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter, would he also be relying upon the same translations that you were receiving from the translator, whether it was Svetlana or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With regard to the translator Svetlana am I correct that she was ethnically of Croatian origin?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, relation to potential problems with the translations that you relied upon, I would like to revisit something you were asked to testify about in the Popovic case. First of all, do you recall being asked about a conversation that you had with General Gvero and whether he actually issued a threat to shell the Potocari UN compound if you do not cease bombing the VRS with NATO planes?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that a question about this was asked when I was testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, that you were presented with the notes of Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter as well as a purported intercept of the conversation which did not, in fact, have the language of that threat as you had initially stated at that trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see it in e-court. I don't know if we have a line and page Mr. Ivetic can provide perhaps for

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, a source?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 1D926 which is the 29th of November, 2007, transcript page 18513, it's page 69 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can perhaps focus at line 18 and onwards, sir. And perhaps for purposes of the translation I will read the pertinent section and it goes as follows: "Mr. Josse: We can put this on the ELMO, Your Honour. It's unmarked. "A. I've read it. "Q. General Gvero did not say to you that he would have the compound at Potocari and the surrounding areas shelled, did he? "A. All I know is what Svetlana interpreted for me. If these transcriptions are correct, and I'm happy to assume that they are, then he did not say it in so many words during that conversation." And then we go to the next page. "Q. If we go back, please, to page 1, at the bottom, it, the relevant part, would appear to be 'thirdly, in case General Nicolai doesn't order the bombing to stop, and doesn't withdraw NATO air planes, he will have personal responsibility for further developments and for the destiny of all people in the area.' "A. Yes, that's correct. That's how it reads and what I understood at the time. "Q. What was the threat in those words? "A. I've explained that as being shelling the compound and the surroundings with the civilian population gathered there." Now, sir, does this refresh your recollection and do you stand by the testimony from the Popovic proceeding that I've just read out to you as to -- as to this selection?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly stand by this. It corresponds with what I answered in previous questions. General Gvero did not state directly in so many words that he would order bombings but he did say that I would be held personally responsible for the subsequent course of events concerning the persons in the enclave, and I interpreted that based in part on the events at the end of May and threats that had apparently been received in the enclave as well, that this would refer to bombings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, with the benefit of hindsight that there was no actual threat voiced by General Gvero, would you agree with me that this notion of a threat did not come from anyone from the VRS but, rather, it was the result of being suggested to you either by the Croatian translator Svetlana or by the DutchBat commander, Colonel Karremans himself?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I'm convinced that this had nothing to do with the quality of the translation by my interpreter Svetlana. At that point throughout the day the city of Srebrenica had been shelled so it was not strange at all to assume that since the city had been abandoned by DutchBat that the firing would be transferred to the compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have just one follow-up question before we lose this train of thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, apart from your Croatian translator Svetlana and Colonel Karremans, did any VRS source ever voice a threat to shell the Potocari compound to you directly?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember specifically but on that day, I did learn from DutchBat that a threat had been received there, that something like that might happen. And that was communicated to me in some way. And that certainly didn't surprise me, given the experience that both the OPs and the compound and the city of Srebrenica had regularly been shelled and shot at earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours we can have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we would adjourn for the day and I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn and resume tomorrow, Friday, 3rd of May, 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of May, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.17 p.m.,
